cases.name: mint-writes-a-claim
cases.notes: §2.1 / §5.4 (17.0): every id the core mints lands in `id_claims` in the commit's transaction, `minted_at = ts` — `d_0` with the doc row (step 2), `r_0` with the head (step 6), `b_0`…`b_2` with the block rows (step 9) — and the recorder's capture sets bit 1 on each (`holders = 3`): the `revisions` row names the head and the document, the `block_changes` rows the blocks. The repo's own `rp_0` claim is not projected (§9.4). `c_0` has no claim: the commit row is the recorder's own evidence.

cases.name: deleted-block-stays-claimed-after-pool-expiry
cases.notes: §2.1 (17.0): the second observation deletes the second paragraph — `b_2` is pooled with `deleted_at` = the deleting commit's ts and `expires_ts = deleted_at + 30 days` (I6 over the row's own timestamp) — and the sweep 31 days later removes the pool row. The claim stays, `holders = 3`: nothing but the prune (§7.3) releases the core's hold and nothing but `history purge` the recorder's. The third observation mints a new paragraph as `b_3`, never `b_2`: the id is in use while its claim exists, with or without a row. Through 16.x the same guarantee rested on the block's earliest `block_changes` row.

cases.name: prune-releases-the-core-hold-and-keeps-the-recorders
cases.notes: §7.3 (17.0): after the delete and the pool sweep, a `gc` with no `identity.claims_retain_days` releases nothing (`claims_released: 0`, the default policy is never). The `exec` step sets the repo's `identity.claims_retain_days` to 30 and the `gc` at T1 + 45 days releases the core's hold on exactly the claims minted before the window that name no core row — `b_2` (no `blocks` row, no pool row) and `r_0` (no longer the head): `claims_released: 2`, both left at `holders = 2` because the recorder's `block_changes`/`revisions` rows still name them, so neither id can be re-minted while history is on. `d_0` (its doc row), `b_0`/`b_1` (live rows) and `r_1` (the head) keep `holders = 3` whatever their age.

sql: UPDATE repos SET settings = '{"identity":{"claims_retain_days":30}}' WHERE repo_id = 'rp_0'

cases.name: pruned-claim-with-no-holder-is-deleted
cases.notes: §7.3 (17.0), the documented consequence (D5): the `exec` step removes the recorder's evidence for `b_2` — its `dispositions`/`block_changes` rows and the recorder's bit on its claim, what `history purge` does for every id (Phase 3e), or what a repository that never captured would have — so the prune's release leaves `b_2` with `holders = 0` and the row is DELETED; `r_0` (still named by its `revisions` row) is released to `holders = 2` as in the sibling case (`claims_released: 2`). With no claim row the probe of §2.1 no longer knows `b_2`: the next production mint MAY return it again (a reused id can only misdirect an unguarded read by name — every guarded write fails `stale_expectation`/`target_missing`). The sequential fixture minter never re-offers an id, so the re-mint itself is pinned by the reference's unit tests (`claims.test.ts`), not here; what this case pins is the row's absence.

sql: UPDATE repos SET settings = '{"identity":{"claims_retain_days":30}}' WHERE repo_id = 'rp_0'
UPDATE id_claims SET holders = holders & ~2 WHERE id = 'b_2'

cases.name: tombstone-and-revival-keep-every-claim
cases.notes: §5.6 / §2.1 (17.0): a vanished file tombstones the document (its three blocks pooled with `deleted_at` = the tombstone's ts, the head `r_0` kept) and the re-creation of the same bytes a minute later resurrects all three out of the pool under a new head `r_1`. No claim moves: `d_0`, `b_0`, `b_1`, `b_2` were claimed at T0 and are carried, not re-minted; the revival's head is the one new claim. (The deleting commit `c_1` has no claim of its own — the recorder's.)
